Below is the memo. I have not written it to disk because I have no tools this turn. Save it at `home-water-reports-trial/causal-design.md`. Nothing has been fitted and no data were inspected.

**Summary:**
- **Primary design:** treat this as the cluster-randomized trial it is, with 12 report towns against 12 comparison towns. The estimand is the effect of *mailing* the reports. With no read records, the effect of *reading* them cannot be estimated.
- **Rebate sign-up must stay out of the adjustment set.** The reports changed sign-up, so controlling for it removes part of the effect and can introduce bias.
- **Precision comes from the 24 towns.** The random draw assigned towns, so 2.1 million reads do not mean 2.1 million independent experiments. Standard errors that treat them that way will be badly understated.
- **The drought order does not need its own adjustment.** It hit both arms, and the random comparison handles it. A before/after comparison within the report towns alone would mix the reports with the drought and the season.

```markdown
# Causal design: monthly home water-use reports trial

Status date: 2026-11-12. Pre-estimation memo. No data have been inspected, no
model has been fitted, and no diagnostic is reported as passed. All facts come
from the project description unless marked otherwise.

## 1. Decision and requested estimand

**Result:** the board's question is a cluster-randomized intention-to-treat
(ITT) question. It is **plausibly identified** by the town-level random draw.
The recommended primary analysis is a town-level randomized comparison of
post-period household water use. It adjusts for prespecified pre-trial
covariates (chiefly pre-period use), and its inference is based on the
randomization of 24 towns. Rebate sign-up is not adjusted for.

- **Requested causal question:** the intervention is mailing a monthly
  neighbor-comparison report to every household in a town. The comparator is
  no new communication. The outcome is household metered water use, with
  monthly use averaged over March 2025 – February 2026. The population is
  households in the 24 smart-meter trial towns. Time zero is the first
  mailing, March 2025. The horizon is 12 months. The contrast is a difference
  in mean monthly use per household, with a percent-of-control-mean summary
  as a secondary scale. The decision the effect informs is not stated. It is
  assumed to be whether to continue or expand the reports (§9).
- **Requested estimand:** ITT of town assignment to reports. This is the
  difference between two quantities among baseline-cohort households in the
  24 trial towns:
  - mean monthly use over the 12 months if their town is mailed reports;
  - mean monthly use if it is not.

  Notation: τ = E[Ȳ_i(1) − Ȳ_i(0)], where Ȳ_i is household i's average
  monthly use over Mar 2025 – Feb 2026. The average is household-weighted
  (assumed; see §9). The effect includes every pathway the reports trigger,
  including rebate sign-up. It is the effect under the conditions that held
  that year, including the July 2025 drought order.
- **Design status for that estimand:** `plausibly identified`. Assignment was
  randomized at the town level, everyone in a report town was mailed, and no
  one could opt out. Outcomes are metered administratively for all
  households. Three things remain to verify:
  - the draw records;
  - mailing fidelity;
  - that outcome observation (closures, vacancies, estimated reads) does not
    differ by arm.

  If missing or estimated reads differ by arm, the status becomes
  `conditional` (§4).
- **Supported alternative estimands (separate; not the board's question):**
  - *Effect of reading the reports:* `not identified`. There is no measure of
    reading, so no first stage exists. Assignment-as-instrument cannot be
    used without a receipt measure. The exclusion restriction would also be
    doubtful, because a report can be glanced at, partially read, or
    discussed.
  - *Effect of the reports in all 58 towns:* not identified from this trial
    alone. The trial towns were selected for having smart meters, so a
    transport argument and data on effect modifiers are needed.
  - *Direct effect of reports not via rebate sign-up:* a mediation question.
    It needs specialist assumptions about rebate sign-up, which is confounded
    by unmeasured household motivation. It is not recommended now.
  - *Month-by-month ITT, including before and after the July 2025 drought
    order:* identified by the same randomization. It describes how the
    effect varied over time. It does not isolate an effect "without the
    drought".
- **Recommendation-changing conditions:**
  - Assignment was not actually random, or was overridden.
  - Comparison towns received report-like communication.
  - Outcome missingness or estimated reads differ by arm.
  - The board wants a 58-town effect or a reading effect.

  Estimation should wait only for the randomization-record and cohort
  definition checks in §7.

Sources: Hernán and Robins (2020), on ITT in randomized designs and
consistency (https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook).

## 2. Design and data inventory

| Fact | Known / assumed / unknown | Evidence / source | Implication / action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 of 58 towns eligible (smart meters); 12 randomly drawn for reports | Known | Project description | The randomization unit is the town. Obtain the draw record: method, seed, date, any strata or restrictions. |
| Draw was simple complete randomization of 12 of 24, with no strata | Assumed | None | Randomization inference must reproduce the actual scheme. If strata or rerandomization were used, change the permutation set. |
| Every household in report towns mailed monthly from March 2025; no opt-out | Known | Project description | Assignment ≈ offer = mailing. Verify mailing logs: undeliverable mail, missed months, new accounts added. |
| Comparison towns got nothing new | Known (claimed) | Project description | Verify no report-like messaging, pilot leakage, or town-specific campaigns in comparison towns. |
| Who read reports | Unknown, unrecorded | Project description | A reading/receipt effect cannot be identified. |
| Towns are separate communities ≥10 miles apart | Known | Project description | Cross-town spillover is plausibly small. Regional media coverage remains possible (§4). |
| Monthly meter reads, all households, 24 towns, Mar 2023 – Feb 2026, ~2.1M reads | Known | Project description | This gives 24 pre-period months for baseline adjustment and checks. Count is ≈2.1M / 36 ≈ 58k households if the panel is complete (rough; to verify). |
| Reads are actual reads aligned to consumption months | Assumed | None | Confirm read dates, billing-cycle offsets, estimated vs actual flags. Normalize to use per day if cycle lengths vary. |
| Smart meters in place for the whole pre-period | Unknown | None | A meter changeover in 2023–24 could change measurement. This matters for baseline adjustment and pre-period checks. |
| Household size, lot size from billing records | Known | Project description | Use as precision covariates only if recorded before March 2025. Confirm the date. |
| Rebate sign-up higher in report towns | Known (descriptive) | Project description | Sign-up is a post-assignment outcome and mediator. Exclude it from adjustment. Report it as a secondary ITT outcome. |
| Drought order, July 2025, all 58 towns | Known | Project description | Common to both arms, so it is not a confounder of the randomized contrast. It is a confounder of any before/after comparison. It may modify the effect. |
| Households moving in or out, vacancies, account closures during the trial | Unknown | None | Defines the cohort and the outcome-observation process. Check by arm. |
| Town-specific concurrent events (rate changes, main breaks, local restrictions) | Unknown | None | With 12 towns per arm, one event can move an arm mean. Inventory these events. They do not break identification but affect precision and interpretation. |
| Data location | Known | Warehouse; not in repo | Extraction is an implementation step. Polars for profiling. |

**Field roles (provisional):**

| Role | Fields | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Keys | town ID; household/account ID; premise ID | — |
| Assignment | town arm Z ∈ {0, 1} | set before March 2025 |
| Outcome | monthly use Y_it | each month; post-period Mar 2025 – Feb 2026 |
| Baseline covariates | household size, lot size; pre-period use Mar 2023 – Feb 2025 | before March 2025 |
| Post-assignment variables | rebate sign-up and date; account status; read type | during the trial |

**Additional data required:**
- the randomization record;
- mailing logs;
- an account start/stop history;
- read-type flags;
- a list of town-level events and policies Mar 2023 – Feb 2026.

## 3. Causal structure and adjustment

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Draw[Random draw, before Mar 2025] --> Z[Town assigned reports Z]
    Z --> Mail[Reports mailed monthly from Mar 2025]
    Mail --> Read[Household reads report: unobserved]
    Read --> Y[Monthly use, Mar 2025 - Feb 2026]
    Read --> Reb[Rebate sign-up]
    Reb --> Y
    U[Unobserved household motivation / attitudes: unobserved] --> Read
    U --> Reb
    U --> Y
    X[Baseline: hh size, lot size, pre-period use] --> Y
    X --> Reb
    T[Town traits: climate, housing, prices] --> X
    T --> Y
    Dr[Drought order Jul 2025, all towns] --> Y
    Dr --> Reb
    Y -.-> O[Read observed / account active]
    Z -.-> O
    Sel[Smart-meter selection of 24 towns] --> Trial[Trial sample]
```

**Node timing:**
- The draw, Z, X and T precede March 2025.
- Mail, Read, Reb and Y are monthly over Mar 2025 – Feb 2026.
- The drought node starts July 2025.
- O is monthly.
- U and Read are unobserved.

**Defended absent edges:**
- *T → Z and X → Z:* none, because of the random draw. This is the key
  design restriction. It is an exact absence if the draw was implemented as
  described.
- *Z → Y other than via mailed reports:* none, assuming nothing else differed
  by arm. Verify.
- *Z in one town → Y in another:* none (spillover); plausible given distance.
  Disputed only for regional media.

**Disputed edges:**
- *Z → O and Y → O* (dashed): could reports change account closure, meter
  estimation, or vacancy? Unlikely, but if outcome observation differs by
  arm, a complete-case analysis conditions on O.

**Target pathway:** all paths from Z to Y, including Z → … → Reb → Y.

**Proposed adjustment set:** none is required for identification. For
precision, prespecify baseline covariates:
- pre-period mean use (household or town);
- household size and lot size, if recorded before March 2025;
- calendar-month effects.

**Exclusions:**
- *Rebate sign-up.* It is a mediator, so adjusting removes the part of the
  effect that works through rebates. It is also a collider on
  Z → Reb ← U → Y, so conditioning on it opens a path between assignment and
  unmeasured motivation. That biases even the "direct" comparison.
- *Any household-level variable measured after March 2025.*
- *Post-period account status as a filter.* Use a baseline-defined cohort
  instead (§7).

**The drought order** needs no adjustment in the randomized contrast. It is
common to both arms and independent of Z. It does confound the analyst's
before/after comparison: post-March use falls with the drought, the season
and secular trends whether or not reports exist.

**Design restriction not encoded in the graph:** the randomization mechanism
itself. Inference must follow the actual draw over 24 towns.

## 4. Identification assumptions and evidence

| Assumption | Why needed | Supporting evidence | Planned challenge / sensitivity | Untestable remainder or gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized assignment of towns (Z independent of potential outcomes) | Exchangeability for ITT | Description of a random draw | Obtain the draw record. Compare pre-period use levels and trends by arm (descriptive check of implementation and chance imbalance). | Gate: the draw record must exist. Balance checks cannot prove the draw was honest; they only describe chance imbalance. |
| Consistency: "mailed monthly reports" is one intervention | Defines τ | Uniform monthly mailing to all households | Mailing logs: report version changes, missed months, undeliverables | If the content changed mid-trial, the ITT is for the program as delivered. Document versions. |
| No contamination of comparison towns | Comparator is "nothing new" | Claimed | Audit utility communications, media, websites by town | If contaminated, τ is a diluted contrast. Report as such. |
| No interference across towns | Each town's outcomes depend only on its own Z | Towns ≥10 miles apart, separate communities | Ask about regional press and shared social networks | Untestable. Spillover would bias τ toward zero. Within-town spillover is part of the town-level treatment and is fine. |
| Positivity | Both arms possible for each town | 12/12 by design | None needed | Satisfied by design. |
| Outcome observation not differentially affected by Z | Complete outcomes for the cohort | Administrative meter reads for all households | Compare the share of missing reads, estimated reads and closed accounts by arm and month | Gate: if differential, status → `conditional`. Use bounds or sensitivity for exits. Equal rates do not prove ignorability. |
| Stable measurement across arms and time | Comparable Y | Same utility metering | Check meter installation dates, read-type flags, billing-cycle changes by arm | A measurement change aligned with assignment would bias the result. Investigate if found. |

These assumptions identify the household-weighted ITT of mailing reports in
the 24 trial towns over Mar 2025 – Feb 2026. They do not identify:
- the effect of reading;
- an effect in all 58 towns;
- the effect without the drought;
- the direct effect excluding rebates.

**Identification versus precision:** the design identifies τ, but precision is
governed by 24 independently assigned towns and between-town variability, not
by 2.1M reads. Treating reads as independent would understate uncertainty,
plausibly by a large factor. Within-household and within-town correlation over
time is strong for water use.

## 5. Candidate comparison and primary choice

| Candidate | Identified estimand | Match to requested target | Critical assumptions | Required data | Main threat | Feasibility / failure action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Cluster-randomized ITT with baseline adjustment (primary)** | Household-weighted ITT of town assignment, 24 towns, 12 months | Direct match | Randomization, no contamination, no cross-town interference, non-differential outcome observation | Town arm; post-period use; pre-period use; baseline covariates | Low precision with 24 clusters; chance imbalance; differential attrition | Feasible. If attrition differs by arm, add bounds. If the draw cannot be verified, treat the design as observational (C). |
| **B. Randomized difference-in-differences (robustness)** | Same ITT, estimated as the difference in change from pre to post | Direct match | Same as A. Randomization makes parallel trends hold in expectation. | Same as A | Less efficient than ANCOVA when pre/post correlation is below 1. Same small-cluster inference issue. | Report alongside A. Material disagreement signals chance imbalance or measurement change; investigate. |
| **C. Analyst's household before/after with rebate control** | Within report towns only: none. Change confounded by drought, season, trend. With comparison towns and household fixed effects: a DiD, but biased by rebate adjustment and with invalid SEs. | Does not answer the question as specified | Would require no drought, season or trend change (false). Rebate adjustment conditions on a mediator/collider. | Same data | Drought order July 2025; seasonality; rebate collider; 2.1M reads treated as independent | Not recommended. Its useful element, household pre-period baselines, is retained in A and B. |

Out of scope here: the reading effect (no receipt measure; would need new
data, e.g. tracked email reports or a survey) and the 58-town effect (would
need effect-modifier data on non-trial towns, or a new randomized rollout).

**Primary:** A.

**Weakest assumption:** no contamination or spillover into comparison towns,
together with non-differential outcome observation. Both are mostly untestable
and checkable only through audit.

**Fallback:** B if pre-period alignment makes ANCOVA awkward. Bounds on τ if
attrition differs by arm. Descriptive-only reporting if the draw record cannot
be verified.

## 6. Diagnostic, falsification and sensitivity plan

All checks are **planned**; none has been performed.

| Check | Data needed | Assumption it can challenge | Limitation | Action if it fails |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Randomization record audit | Draw procedure, seed, date, strata | Random assignment; correct permutation set | Cannot detect undocumented overrides | If unverifiable, downgrade to observational comparison and say so |
| Pre-period balance by arm: levels and trends of use, household size, lot size, Mar 2023 – Feb 2025 | Pre-period reads, covariates | Draw implementation; size of chance imbalance | With 12 per arm, chance imbalance is expected; balance cannot test unobservables | Rely on prespecified baseline adjustment. Report imbalance. Do not re-select covariates after seeing outcomes. |
| Placebo ITT: Mar 2024 – Feb 2025 as fake post period, same estimator | Pre-period reads | Implementation errors; measurement changes; analysis code | Absence of a placebo effect does not certify the real estimate | Investigate the data pipeline and measurement before trusting the main result |
| Mailing fidelity | Mailing logs, return-to-sender counts by town and month | Consistency; dose | Logs do not show reading | Document the delivered program. τ remains the ITT of assignment. |
| Comparison-town contamination audit | Communications records, media | No contamination / interference | Absence of records ≠ absence of exposure | Interpret τ as a lower-bound-type contrast. Note in claims. |
| Outcome-observation check by arm and month: missing, estimated and zero reads, closures, new accounts | Account history, read flags | Non-differential observation | Equal rates do not prove ignorable missingness | If differential: bounds (e.g. trimming or worst case) with stated assumptions; restrict claims |
| Measurement stability: meter install dates, billing-cycle changes | Meter records | Stable outcome measurement | May be incompletely recorded | Restrict the pre-period used for adjustment; report |
| Inference sensitivity: randomization inference vs small-sample cluster-robust (CR2, Satterthwaite df) vs wild cluster bootstrap | Town-level statistics | Inference validity with 24 clusters | Methods differ in the null they test; randomization CIs need an effect model, e.g. constant additive | Report all. If they disagree, lead with randomization inference. |
| Weighting sensitivity: household-weighted vs town-weighted ITT | Town household counts | None (different estimands) | They answer different questions | Report both if they differ. Board chooses the target (§9). |
| Month-by-month ITT (descriptive heterogeneity, incl. post-drought) | Monthly reads | None for identification | Many comparisons; low power per month | Treat as secondary. Do not claim a "drought-free effect". |
| Secondary outcome: ITT on rebate sign-up | Rebate records | None (it is a separate outcome) | Explains mechanism only descriptively | Report separately. Do not use as a covariate. |
| Influence of single towns: leave-one-town-out | Town-level data | Sensitivity of the result to one town's concurrent event | Does not identify which event | Report instability. Check the event inventory for that town. |

**What passed diagnostics cannot prove:**
- no unmeasured contamination;
- no spillover;
- ignorable attrition;
- that the draw was not tampered with.

## 7. Implementation handoff

**Estimand and sample:**

| Field | Specification |
|---|---|
| Requested estimand | τ, the household-weighted ITT of town assignment to monthly reports, per §1 |
| Secondary estimands | town-weighted ITT; percent effect relative to the comparison-arm mean; month-specific ITTs; ITT on rebate sign-up |
| Population/cohort | Households with an active residential account in a trial town at baseline. Assumed: active in February 2025 and with at least one pre-period read. |
| Accounts opened after March 2025 | Excluded from the primary cohort; sensitivity analysis includes them |
| Non-residential accounts | Excluded (assumed not mailed) |
| Intervention / comparator | Town assigned to mailed reports vs. not |
| Outcome | Household average metered use per month (or per day, if read cycles vary) over Mar 2025 – Feb 2026, in the warehouse's volume units. Prespecify the treatment of estimated and zero reads. |
| Time zero / horizon | March 2025 / 12 months |

**Data:**
- Warehouse extracts:
  - read table (account, premise, town, read date, service period, volume, read type);
  - account history (start, stop, residential flag);
  - billing covariates with record dates;
  - rebate table (account, sign-up date);
  - town assignment;
  - mailing logs.
- Keys: town ID (cluster/assignment unit); account and premise IDs; service month.
- Profile in Polars.

**Gates before estimation (stop if unmet):**
1. Randomization record confirms 12-of-24 random assignment and its scheme.
2. Cohort and outcome definitions are frozen in writing before looking at
   post-period arm differences.
3. Outcome-observation check (§6) is done. If observation differs by arm,
   specify bounds before estimating.
4. Comparison-town contamination audit is done.

**Estimator (primary):**
- Compute each household's post-period mean monthly use and pre-period mean
  monthly use.
- Analyse at the assignment level with a town-level estimator. For example,
  run a regression of household post-period mean use on Z, adjusting for
  pre-period mean use, household size and lot size (prespecified, baseline
  only). It is weighted so that it targets the household-weighted ITT, with
  inference clustered by town.
- Equivalently, compute town-level covariate-adjusted means and difference
  them with household-count weights.
- With unequal town sizes, a household-weighted difference in means is a
  ratio-type estimator. State which estimator is used and check its
  sensitivity against the town-weighted version.
- **Do not include rebate sign-up or any post-March-2025 variable.**
- Robustness (B): the town-level difference in pre-to-post change, with
  months aligned by calendar month to remove seasonality.

**Inference:**
- Primary: randomization inference over the actual assignment set. Under
  simple 12-of-24 randomization, all C(24,12) = 2,704,156 assignments, or a
  large random subset, using the same adjusted statistic. Confidence
  intervals come from test inversion under a stated effect model, such as a
  constant additive effect.
- Secondary: CR2 cluster-robust SEs with small-sample degrees of freedom, and
  a wild cluster bootstrap at the town level.
- Effective sample size is 24 clusters. Read-level or household-level
  conventional SEs are invalid and must not be reported as the main
  uncertainty.
- Multiplicity: one primary outcome and horizon. Label month-specific and
  subgroup results exploratory.

**Bayesian execution:** `not applicable` by default. The design-based
randomization analysis is sufficient. If a hierarchical model is wanted later
(e.g. partial pooling of month-specific effects), use
`recommend-probabilistic-model` to choose it in `recommendation.md` beside
this memo, then `bayesian-workflow` (NumPyro/JAX). Identification still rests
on randomization, not on priors.

**Output specification:**
- τ with its randomization-based interval, plus secondary inference methods.
- Absolute and percent scales.
- Household- vs town-weighted results.
- Placebo-period result, balance tables, attrition-by-arm table,
  leave-one-town-out plot, monthly ITT plot, and rebate-sign-up ITT.

**Claim limits:**
- This is the effect of *mailing* reports, in 24 smart-meter towns, during a
  drought year.
- It is not the effect of reading, not a 58-town effect, and not a
  drought-free effect.

**Implementation pointers:** randomization-inference and small-cluster
inference references are not in this skill's verified source list; verify
current primary documentation before citing (§8).

## 8. Sources

- Hernán, M. A., and J. M. Robins (2020). *Causal Inference: What If.*
  Author's book page: https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook. Cited for
  ITT/randomized designs, consistency, exchangeability, positivity, selection
  through conditioning on post-treatment variables, and the distinction
  between assignment and receipt. No chapter locators used.
- Lopez Bernal, J., S. Cummins, A. Gasparrini (2017). *Interrupted time series
  regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial.*
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5407170/. Cited for why a
  before/after comparison is vulnerable to seasonality and concurrent events
  such as the drought order.
- **Source uncertainty:** primary references for cluster-randomized
  randomization inference and small-sample cluster-robust inference (CR2,
  wild cluster bootstrap) were not verified in this session. The implementer
  should verify and add them before citing.

## 9. Open questions and next action

| Question | Who/what can answer | Effect on recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| What decision does the estimate inform (continue, expand to 58 towns, budget)? Does a trial-town ITT answer it? | Board / program owner | If expansion to non-smart-meter towns is the decision, add a transport analysis or a new randomized rollout |
| Household-weighted or town-weighted effect? (Assumed household-weighted) | Board | Changes the primary estimator weights |
| How was the draw done (seed, strata, rerandomization), and is it documented? | Analyst / program owner | Defines the randomization-inference set. If undocumented, downgrades the design. |
| Did comparison towns get any report-like communication, media coverage or pilot messaging? | Communications team | Contamination dilutes τ and changes interpretation |
| Were mailings complete and the report content stable for all 12 months? | Program owner / mailing vendor | Defines the delivered intervention |
| Cohort: how should move-ins, move-outs, vacancies and new accounts be handled? Do they differ by arm? | Analyst, from account history | Differential attrition → `conditional` status and bounds |
| Are reads actual or estimated, aligned to service month, and were smart meters in place throughout 2023–24? | Metering/billing team | Outcome definition and baseline validity |
| Were household size and lot size recorded before March 2025? | Billing team | Eligibility as baseline covariates |
| Any town-specific rate changes, restrictions or infrastructure events in 2023–2026? | Operations | Interpretation and leave-one-town-out checks |
| Was the rebate program offered equally in all towns? | Program owner | Confirms rebate sign-up is a downstream outcome, not a separate arm difference |

**Next action:** resolve the randomization-record and cohort questions above,
freeze the outcome and cohort definitions, then begin implementation in a fresh
session using this memo as the input.
```

---

**For your analyst:** keeping each household's pre-period use is a good idea, and it is retained as a precision covariate. The three changes are:
1. Compare against the 12 comparison towns rather than only before/after.
2. Drop rebate sign-up as a control.
3. Base the standard errors on the 24 towns.

The questions in §9 can be answered in any order. The randomization record and the cohort definition are the two that should come before any estimation.
